<design_philosophy>
You are building ONE explorable web page for a research result. The reader should come away
having SEEN the result in the run's own data, because they operated it: they switched between
the conditions the run compared, dragged a threshold and watched the numbers move, pointed at a
mark to see which model or item it was, filtered down to the cases where the method failed, and
put an input beside its output. The page explains through interaction. It is not the paper with
nicer CSS, not a list of headline numbers, and not a gallery of the paper's figures.

WHAT EARNS AN INTERACTION
Every control answers a question a reader actually has at that point, and it changes a view drawn
from the run's real data:
- "Does it hold everywhere?" A chart of the per-condition, per-model or per-dataset results with a
  control over which ones are shown; the baseline always visible; pointing at a mark shows that
  record in full.
- "What does it do to one case?" An item browser over the real per-item records: filter, search
  or sort, and the selected item shows its input, the method's output, the baseline's output and
  the verdict side by side, as a before and after.
- "Where does it break?" A toggle that isolates the failures, the disagreements or the hardest
  slice, with the counts updating as it changes.
- "What if?" A slider over a parameter the recorded data lets the page recompute honestly, such as
  a decision threshold applied to the recorded per-item scores, with the metrics recomputed live.
- "Can I try it?" A live mini-demo of the method, only when the method runs exactly in a few
  dozen lines of JavaScript; it runs on the embedded examples and shows that its output matches
  the recorded one.
- "How does it work?" A stepper that walks ONE real example through the method's stages with the
  values recorded at each stage, over a pipeline diagram that highlights the current stage.
- "What does this word mean?" Term tooltips on hover, focus and tap, with a glossary.
Do not add an interaction that answers no question: no animated counters, no parallax, no
autoplaying carousel, no toggle that swaps one paragraph for a synonym of itself.

THE DATA IS REAL, OR IT IS NOT ON THE PAGE
Every data point comes from the run's output files, embedded as the file has it or trimmed to
the fields a view uses, and every number the prose states matches the paper. A view may compute
from real data (a mean, a filter, a threshold swept over recorded scores), but nothing is ever
invented, interpolated, simulated or smoothed to make a control feel richer. A page that looks
excellent and misreports one result is worse than no page.

ONE STORY
Top to bottom the page tells one story: the question, the answer shown in a view the reader can
operate at once, how the method works, the evidence to explore, where it fails, and what it does
not show. Each view opens with the question it answers and closes with one takeaway sentence
that rewrites itself to describe what the current selection shows.

CRAFT
- Type carries the design: one system font stack, a real scale with visible jumps between levels,
  body text around 17-19px with a measure of 65-75 characters and generous line height.
- Colour is restrained: a light, near-white ground, one dark ink for text, one accent for links,
  the active state and the highlighted series, a muted second colour for baselines, and a
  colour-blind-safe palette when series need more. No gradients as decoration, no purple-to-blue
  banner, no emoji, no icon fonts.
- Charts are read, not decorated: labelled axes with units, a legend when there is more than one
  series, gridlines light enough to recede, and the exact value one hover, focus or tap away.
- Controls look like controls: a visible affordance, a visible selected state, a visible focus
  ring, and a hit area of at least 40 by 40 pixels on a phone.
- Motion is a courtesy: short transitions on state changes only, and none at all under
  prefers-reduced-motion.
- Every interactive element works with a keyboard and tells a screen reader what it is and what
  state it is in. That is part of the craft, not a checklist bolted on at the end.

FINISH IT
The page is done when you have opened it in a headless browser, operated every control, seen no
script error, read it at a phone width and a desktop width, and found nothing to fix. Not before.
</design_philosophy>

  summary: >-
    Experiment 3 screens candidate C, a text-free, gold-free consensus metric for NL->FOL faithfulness, on the shared frozen
    screen (label hash 0e43cbdd...). c_score = 1 - eq_frac: the share of OTHER systems' translations of the same sentence
    that are NOT z3-equivalent to the candidate modulo vocabulary alignment. The pool has 6 fresh OpenRouter families (llama-3.3-70b,
    qwen3-235b, deepseek-v3.1, mistral-small-3.2, gemini-2.5-flash-lite, gpt-4.1-mini) plus the 3 released Logic-LM systems,
    leave-one-out. Also scored: medoid repair depth and operators, and semantic entropy over z3 classes. Baselines: K=5 self-consistency
    (gpt-4.1-nano T=0.7 on all items; true same-model gpt-3.5-turbo SC for gpt-3.5 candidates), predicate-set stability, and
    FOL length. PRIMARY (track L, 297 CORRECT vs 249 ERROR, sentence-clustered bootstrap 2000): c_score AUROC 0.866 [0.821,
    0.906]; peers-only 0.872; non-OpenAI peers 0.863; other Logic-LM systems only 0.753; cluster entropy 0.773; medoid depth
    0.722; sc5_cheap 0.725 [0.669, 0.781] (n=546, now complete). Paired Δ c_score - sc5_cheap = +0.140 [0.085, 0.197]; c_score
    - sc5_same = +0.140 [0.057, 0.227] (n=167). Cross-fitted [c_score, sc5] vs [sc5] = +0.147. Vocab-clean subset (shared-aligner
    confound control): c_score 0.852 vs SC 0.714. At the medoid threshold: recall 0.62, false alarms 0.14. Shared blind spot:
    38% of errors are endorsed by the consensus (POLARITY 5%, COVERAGE 41%, STRUCT 57%). Repair operators match the labeller's
    81% of the time (chance 46%). RENAME rewrites cause 96% false alarms (the aligner does not survive synonym or constant
    renaming); z3-equivalent rewrites flip 0% by construction. Long/conditioned stratum n=5, descriptive only. Cost: $1.52
    total; the peer pool costs $0.0015 per sentence. This re-run completed the SC_cheap arm that the shared-key limit had
    cut to 231/307 units, and restored WordNet for RENAME.

    (bootstrap cluster), item_id, strata {words,n_quant,depth,n_conditions,exception_type,source_stratum,l25_topup_batch},
    auto_label, repair_ops, panel_votes, error_ops, label_tier, reference_status, correct_not_equivalent, reading_choice,

    output CORRECT). They cover 300 bases: 36 TRUSTED_AGREED + 95 GOLD_PANEL_OK + 69 PANEL_REPAIRED dataset-E references,
    and 100 R_COMP weak readings. Operators are NEG, REV, QUANT, RESTR, CONN, MOVE, DROP, ADD (ADD_FOREIGN / ADD_INTERNAL),
    SWAP, BIND and MEANING_RENAME, at DOWN/UP positions (metadata_position_polarity, polarity_method, matched_pair_id; 1,354

    accepted reading. Controls are RENAME_SYN / RENAME_NONCE, REORDER and CONTRAPOSITIVE/DEMORGAN, each z3-equivalent. (2)

    a not-accepted converse), are unit-tested and z3-checked, and are built from a 652-entry atom lexicon mined from verified
    FOLIO/MALLS references. Provenance fields: template_id, lexicon_ids, source_rule_ids. CAVEAT: the shared OpenRouter key
    hit its daily limit 5 minutes in ($0.41 spent); the 21:38 UTC replacement key was also already exhausted. Pending: the

- iteration: 3
  name: gen_art_research_1
  type: research
  title: What is new about peer agreement for logic
  summary: >-
    Prior-art positioning (web research, $0 LLM spend, 63 sources, 139 verbatim quotes machine-checked against fetched text)
    for the iteration-3 claim that cross-family solver consensus is a gold-free NL->FOL faithfulness metric. SCOOP RULE (multi-family
    translations + solver equivalence + faithfulness-label meta-eval on NL->FOL): no hit meets all three, so C1 is not scooped.
    Closest neighbours meet two of three each: ARc 2511.09008 (NL->SMT, k LLMs, per-translation confidence = share of k translations
    entailing it, i.e. the same score form as c_score, but a fixed schema and downstream-QA labels); NoTB 2608.21962 (RTL,
    4 families, precision 63/85.3/87/94.7% at >=1..4 families, coverage 100/49/33/27%, spec-level, no AUROC); GenV 2609.11085
    (NL->FOL, single trained verifier, AUROC 0.961 on Z3-reference labels; single-model SC K=5 = 0.863; the judge beats GenV
    0.778 vs 0.679 when labels switch to panel intent). The closest meta-evaluation design is SCP-NL2TL 2608.05439 (NL->temporal
    logic, single-model SC vs judge vs back-translation AUROC by difficulty tier; SC AUROC rises with tier). VERDICTS: C1
    NEEDS-QUALIFIER (the method is not new; claim the first meta-evaluation of cross-family consensus as a per-candidate NL->FOL
    faithfulness score vs an API judge, nested over the baseline stack; win and loss wordings are given); C2 SAFE (cite GenV's
    label-target reversal and wrong-gold rates, 2606.02837 v1 39%/36% vs v2 42.5%/42%); C3 NEEDS-QUALIFIER (predicate alignment
    exists in LogicLLaMA and Vossel; no neighbour reports a rename false-alarm rate); C4 NEEDS-QUALIFIER (balanced-accuracy
    maths; the scatter premise is stated by LLMs-as-Jury, CLOVER and Chen & Avizienis 1978, who noted identical wrong results
    from missing logic; the new piece is a measured identical-wrong vs both-wrong curve over number of conditions, set against
    Eckhardt-Lee's coincident-failure-rises-with-difficulty); C5 NEEDS-QUALIFIER (LLMs-as-Jury already recommend 3-4 cross-family
    models; effective-N results: 7 models ~ 2.58, 9 judges ~ 2). Also supplies: the positioning table on 10 axes; a premise-evidence
    table (60% agree-when-both-wrong on MCQ, rho 0.20-0.59, beta 0.052-0.127, KL 1255 tests); judge-degradation evidence (AutoEval:
    equivalence verification fails beyond toy complexity; >20 operators <50%); cost norms; 8 required extra rows (single-family
    SC, precision@coverage by k, endorsement vs both-wrong by conditions, k-curve per tercile, rename FA per matcher, label-protocol
    sensitivity, n_eff, cite ARc); AuthorYYYY citation strings; and a search log. Files: research_report.md (main), notes/QUOTES.md
    (quote ledger).
  workspace: >-
    /ai-inventor/aii_data/runs/run_u75jRHUss0zo/3_invention_loop/iter_3/gen_art/gen_art_research_1
  output_files:

    T8 (iteration 4) is a CPU-only evaluation: no LLM calls, $0. It never reads the sibling CSC experiment. Eval-2 functions
    are imported unchanged (code sha dd73975642f428cc). E and R_COMP are DEVELOPMENT data, so nothing here is confirmation.

    d_floor (R_point_label, an oracle-assisted prediction) 0.402 [0.336, 0.471]; bracket [0.396, 0.415]; exact-only 0.683;
    no-anchoring oracle floor 0.385 (0.345 with a labelled denominator); e_ceiling 0.162. 9-family: 0.537 / 0.532 / 0.522,
    with oracle 0.586. The pre-registered gap_closed rule is ill-conditioned: its denominator is 0.013. Behind d, 77% (9-family)
    / 61% (3-pool) of non-agreeing peers of CORRECT candidates are labelled ERROR, and only 9% of CORRECT-CORRECT disagreements
    are NF/HYB-resolvable. The specificity placebo shows VOCAB agreements are not label-specific (ratio 1.98 [0.43, 11.4]
    3-pool; 0.83 9-family). c_vres does not beat c_score_align on L25 (-0.014 [-0.028, -0.001]), which predicts that G2 fails.
    NET stays DEGRADES under every rule. PART 2 (R_COMP): SIG e 0.000, d 0.2596 (weak 0.143 / strong 0.965), SCATTER ratio
    4.38. Paired same-slot-pair exact agreement is SIG 0.528 vs FREE 0.048, a drop of +0.479 [0.447, 0.513]. Post-hoc ALIGN
    recovers 41% of it, NF 18%, ALIGN∪NF 45%. The out-of-sample validation of the Part-1 method FAILED: predicted 0.20 vs
    actual SIG endorsement 0.575, calibration error -0.37 [-0.42, -0.32]; Spearman across templates 0.97. So the instruments
    under-count vocabulary effects. PART 3 (power_E2.json): yield is L25 0.37, L20 0.53, EXC 0.64, CTRL 0.25. Planned L25
    250/300/350/400 gives MDE80 0.130/0.119/0.110/0.103, all MARGINAL. Detecting +0.069 needs about 882 planned L25 sentences,
    or about 237 usable sentences in the long pool. R_COMP FREE needs at least 200 CORRECT rows. PART 4: 13 record tables

- iteration: 5
  name: gen_art_experiment_14
  type: experiment
  title: Screening fixes for model-agreement false alarms
  summary: >-
    Iteration-5 FREEZE on dataset E (DEVELOPMENT data; nothing here confirms). PART A ($0): five label-free rescorings of
    frozen V0 = c_score_align, computed only from eval-2's pairwise eqmv matrix, sealed (sha256) before any label join. V1
    plurality-normalised, V2 reliability-weighted (out-of-fold family weights), V3 = V1+V2, V4 cross-fitted exact/align logistic,
    V5 = V3 on the 3-pool. Gates reproduce exactly: G0 V0 strat 0.7415 and Δ +0.099 [0.049, 0.146]; G1 24/8,469 = 0.28% (the
    6-decimal rounding of the frozen column is handled at 1e-6, D1); c_exact 0.748; 3-pool 0.7845; eval-3 oracle 0.385 / 0.542.
    Z = 2,672 rows. LONG-strat AUROC: V0 0.743; Δ V1 -0.004, V2 +0.0075 [0.004, 0.011], V3 +0.007, V4 +0.009 [-0.004, 0.021],
    V5 +0.003. The pre-registered rule (Δ LONG >= +0.015, L25 >= V0, CTRL >= V0 - 0.01) gives 'NONE: V0 stands'. Stability:
    NONE 87.6%, V4 11.8%. Null: some variant qualifies in 3.5% of permutations. Mechanism: plurality normalisation trades
    d for e (ALL d 0.490 -> 0.174, e 0.140 -> 0.343; MEANING_RENAME-type e 0.502 -> 0.872). No variant lowers d without raising
    e. The 9-family oracle gap is ILL_CONDITIONED (d_oracle 0.586 > d_V0 0.490). Marker M1 freeze/CONSENSUS_FREEZE_READY.json
    was written 12 min after the first code, with freeze/selection.json and consensus_variants.py (20-row reproduction to
    1e-9). PART B ($0.22): GG = exact z3 equivalence OR an exhaustive injective arity-consistent symbol map giving z3 equivalence
    AND gemini-2.5-flash (non-thinking) says YES for every renamed pair. Checker gate G-A: dev v1 0.780 fails; the one allowed
    revision v2 scores 0.907 on the confirm half. G-B (R_COMP renames): 0.950 / 0.941, NOT_TESTABLE as a gate with only 53
    YES pairs (D2). Dev gates: g1 SYN paired flip 0.034 and g2 MEANING_RENAME recall 1.0 both pass, trivially because base
    FA is 0.83. g3 FAILS: E ALL-strat 0.696 vs V0 0.742, Δ -0.046 [-0.071, -0.021], so GG = FAIL(g3) and the boundary statement
    is written. GG halves error endorsement (e 0.140 -> 0.081; MEANING_RENAME-type 0.502 -> 0.224) but raises d (0.490 ->
    0.629): all 678 granularity (gran) pairs fail the bijection prefilter and 268 align pairs are gloss-rejected. Cost per
    candidate: 0.038 CPU-s + <= $0.00005. Secondary GG_B (freelab B1-B5 bridges) searched 11,202 pairs; its gloss is UNTESTED(budget)
    because the run-level OpenRouter budget was exhausted (HTTP 403, D13). Its all-accepted bracket is worse (ALL-strat 0.653;
    e 0.334): the bridges absorb ADD/DROP errors. PART C: lib/api.py over byte-identically vendored code (lib/PROVENANCE.json
    sha256), with modes align/exact/nf/hyb/pn/rw/gg, graded_consensus, pairwise_matrix/ed_decomposition, peer_text_score,
    eqmv(+exhaustive), minimal_typed_repair, freelab labelling tools and FOL-Triage layers. smoke_lib.py passes on 10 E rows.

<data_requirements>
- Embed each dataset the views use as its own
  `<script type="application/json" id="data-..." data-source="...">` element, where
  `data-source` names the artifact and the output file it came from (for example
  `experiment_1/method_out.json`), never an absolute path. The inline script reads each one with
  `JSON.parse(document.getElementById(id).textContent)` and builds every chart, table, count and
  control from it; no number a view shows is typed into the markup by hand.
- Produce the embedded JSON with a script that reads the output files, not by copying values, so
  it is exactly what the files hold. Keep only the fields the views use.
- When a file is too large to embed whole, embed a subset chosen by a rule the page states (for
  example every failure plus a seeded random sample of the rest) and the aggregates computed from
  the full file.
- The numbers the prose states match the paper. A view may compute from the embedded data (a
  mean, a filter, a threshold swept over recorded scores), and says so; it never invents,
  interpolates, simulates or smooths a data point.
- Every number the paper states (a headline rate, a confidence interval, a table cell, a p-value)
  appears on the page exactly as the paper states it, at the paper's precision. Embed it from the
  artifact output file that holds it and print that value; never re-derive it in the browser. A
  bootstrap re-run in the page draws different resamples, and a mean recomputed from rounded or
  subsampled rows rounds differently, so a CI of [0.38, 0.68] turns into [0.37, 0.68] and a
  0.364 into 0.363. Where a live view recomputes a quantity the paper states (a threshold sweep,
  a filter over the items), the setting that matches the paper must show the paper's value: take
  that row from the file, or check the live result against it before shipping.
</data_requirements>

<figure_requirements>
- The page draws its own charts from the embedded data; the paper's figures are not its visuals.
  Show at most 3 of them, and only where a figure shows what the data cannot
  (the method diagram, an example rendering), never a data plot the page can draw live.
- Reference a figure as `figures/` plus its filename, exactly as listed above. The
  page and the figures folder are published together, so that relative path resolves on the live
  site and anything else breaks.
- A browser cannot draw a PDF in an image element. For a figure listed as "render from ...
  first", use the PNG of that name in `figures/` when it is already there, and
  otherwise render one there at about 200 DPI with pdftoppm or pymupdf. Renderable formats:
  .avif, .gif, .jpeg, .jpg, .png, .svg, .webp.
- Use the figure's own caption, and look at the figure before placing it.
</figure_requirements>

<page_structure>
Top to bottom:

1. HEADER: the title, the author line as the paper gives it, and the paper link as the primary
   button, labelled "Read the paper (PDF)". The other links from the links section sit beside it.
2. THE FINDING: the question and the answer in plain language, with the single number that
   carries it, and beside them the headline view, operable at once: the result drawn from the
   embedded data, the baseline shown with it, and a control over the conditions it was measured
   under.
3. HOW IT WORKS: a stepper that walks ONE real example from the data through the method's
   stages, showing at each stage what goes in, what is done to it, what comes out (the recorded
   values where the run kept them) and why. A pipeline diagram in inline SVG highlights the
   current stage; previous and next buttons, clickable stage markers and the left and right arrow
   keys move between stages.
4. EXPLORE THE EVIDENCE: two or more views over the real data, chosen from the kinds in the
   design philosophy to fit this result. At least one is an item browser: filter, search or sort
   over the real per-item records, and a detail panel that puts the selected item's input, the
   method's output and the baseline's output (or its before and after) side by side.
5. TRY IT: the live mini-demo when the method runs exactly in the page; otherwise a what-if view
   that sweeps a threshold or parameter over the recorded scores and recomputes the metrics live.
   Leave it out only when neither would be honest for this result, and say why in your summary.
6. WHERE IT FAILS: the failure cases from the data one control away, then what the paper says it
   does not show.
7. FOOTER: every link from the links section again, a data provenance list naming the artifact
   file behind each view, the glossary of every term with a tooltip, and the citation if the
   paper carries one.

A compact section navigation marks where the reader currently is. Each view opens with the
question it answers and ends with a takeaway sentence that updates with the selection.
</page_structure>

<interaction_requirements>
- Controls are real form controls or ARIA widgets: a range input with its current value printed
  beside it, a select, checkboxes, a radio group or tab list, buttons with aria-pressed. Each one
  changes a view without a page jump, and the view's counts and takeaway sentence change with it.
- Charts are inline SVG you generate, or canvas when there are thousands of marks: labelled axes
  with units, bars that start at zero, the baseline always shown, a legend when there is more than
  one series, and values printed at the precision the source has. Every mark shows its record on
  hover, on keyboard focus and on tap.
- Tooltips: each term trigger is a button with the term as its text, showing its definition on
  hover, on keyboard focus and on tap, dismissed by Escape and by tapping elsewhere, and exposed to
  assistive technology through aria-describedby. Define each term from the paper's own wording.
  A mouse click fires hover, focus and click in turn, and a tap fires focus and click, so a click
  handler that toggles closes the definition the moment it opened: every one of those events
  OPENS the tooltip, and only Escape, a click or tap elsewhere, or leaving the trigger closes it.
- Stepper: the current stage is announced through an aria-live region, the buttons disable at
  the ends, and the current stage marker carries aria-current.
- The page works with no network at all and logs no error or warning to the browser console.
</interaction_requirements>

<technical_requirements>
- ONE file: all CSS in a style element and all JavaScript in a script element, both inline in
  `interactive.html`, beside the data elements. No framework, no external script,
  stylesheet, web font or analytics. The only files the page may point at are the figures listed
  above.
- A complete HTML document: the file opens with exactly this markup, then the title and the
  style element, and closes head before the body. Without the viewport tag a phone lays the page
  out 980px wide and shrinks it to tiny text.
```html
<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
```
- Chart text never collides: in every chart, axis titles, tick labels, value labels and legend
  entries each keep their own space at every width. A rotated y-axis title sits left of the
  widest tick label with a gap: size the left margin from the measured label widths (getBBox or
  getComputedTextLength), not from a fixed guess.
- Plain modern JavaScript, no build step.
- Formulas use HTML sub and sup elements or inline MathML. TeX notation such as `^`, `_` or
  `\frac` must not reach the page.
- System font stack only. Light theme.
- Responsive from a 360px phone to a wide desktop with no horizontal page scroll; wide tables and
  charts scroll inside their own container or reflow, and charts redraw to their container width.
- Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
- Keyboard-navigable in a sensible Tab order with a visible focus ring and a skip link to the
  main content.
- Semantic HTML: one top-level heading, headings that descend without skipping, landmark
  elements, and alt text on every image that says what it shows.
- Keep the whole file under 3 MB.
</technical_requirements>

<page_gate>
When you finish, the page is loaded in a headless browser and sent back to you if its script
throws an error; if it has no `application/json` data element that its inline script reads by
id; if it shows more than 3 static images; or if, once its script has run, it
draws fewer than 2 charts (svg or canvas) or offers fewer than 3
controls; if it does not open with the document head above; or if, at 1280px wide, the
text boxes of two labels in one chart overlap (an axis title over a tick label, two legend
entries). It is also sent back if `index.html` is present and does not link to
`interactive.html`.
</page_gate>

<writing_register>
Write in the register of the field's best papers (the paper this page teaches, which was written to them), not in the register of a language
model. Four things are measured on the finished draft, and a draft outside them is sent back with
the numbers:
- Never use: delve, underscore, showcase, intricate, pivotal, realm, commendable, meticulous, tapestry, garner, multifaceted, it is worth noting, plays a crucial role, not only ... but also. These are 10 to 30 times more frequent in machine-written abstracts than in
  human ones, and reviewers read them as such.
- Em dashes: at most 3 per 1,000 words. Use a comma, a colon or a full stop.
- Sentence rhythm: mix short and long sentences. An interquartile range of sentence length under
  8 words reads as machine-written.
- Hedging: at most 15 hedges (may, likely, suggests, appears) per 1,000
  words. State what the evidence supports plainly; hedge where it is thin, not everywhere.
Style never changes substance: numbers, claims, citations and figure markers stay exactly as the
evidence gives them. The user's original request (delivered as a separate message) overrides all
of this wherever the two conflict.
</writing_register>

I work on converting natural-language text into first-order logic (NL→FOL, autoformalization) with
LLM pipelines. Evaluation is the bottleneck. Correct FOL for a sentence is not unique — different
predicate names, different decompositions of the same concept, and logically equivalent rewrites can
all be correct. Gold FOL annotations are rare and expensive. The metrics in use either need a gold
formula (exact match, BLEU, prover-checked equivalence to the gold) or only check that the output
parses. In my own pilot I used cheap structural metrics: whether a set of generated formulas loads
together without conflicts, whether predicate arities stay consistent, how many predicates are used
but never defined, and how similar the predicate sets are across reruns. Those measure stability and
composability, not whether a formula says what the sentence says.

Find new metrics for NL→FOL output quality. Operating situation: you are given a natural-language
sentence (or short passage) and a candidate FOL formalization produced by any system. There is no gold
formula, no ontology or controlled vocabulary, and no domain knowledge. The metric returns a score
that predicts whether the formalization is faithful to the text, and ideally which kind of error it
contains (quantifier or scope error, dropped or added condition, negation/polarity error, swapped
arguments, conflated or wrongly split concepts). Metrics may score a single formula or a set (several
samples for one sentence, or the formalizations of all sentences in one document). They must be
task-agnostic — usable for any NL→FOL setting, not tied to a domain, dataset or pipeline — and cheap
enough to run on every output (solver calls and small models are fine; a large-LLM judge per formula
only if shown to earn its cost).

Requirements:
- Keep the target fixed: the metric must predict faithfulness to the text. Detecting synthetic
  perturbations, parse validity, or run-to-run stability are not substitutes for that target.
- Validate against ground truth, never against the metric itself. Use public datasets with gold
  sentence-level FOL (e.g. FOLIO, MALLS, or others you find) to build a meta-evaluation set: real
  candidate formalizations from several different systems, plus controlled perturbations of gold
  formulas with known error types, labelled via prover-checked equivalence to gold. Handle two known
  problems: some gold annotations are wrong, and a candidate can be correct without being equivalent
  to the gold (different vocabulary or granularity). Estimate how often each happens and how it
  biases the labels. These datasets are public, so check whether LLM-based metrics benefit from having
  seen the gold.
- For each metric report: correlation with correctness at item and system level; sensitivity per error
  type; invariance under meaning-preserving rewrites (variable/predicate renaming, reordering,
  equivalent restatements); coverage — unparseable outputs are counted and reported, never silently
  dropped; and cost.
- Compare against baselines: parse/compile rate, round-trip (FOL→NL→compare) similarity,
  LLM-as-judge, sampling self-consistency, and the structural consistency metrics described above. A
  new metric matters only if it adds signal those don't.
- Report how each metric's reliability changes with sentence complexity (length, number of quantifiers,
  nesting depth, number of conditions and exceptions). Long, heavily conditioned sentences matter most
  to me.
- Negative results are welcome: if a family of metrics does not track correctness, show that clearly.

Out of scope: comparing grounded vs ungrounded generation (ontology vocabulary injected into prompts),
anything that depends on a particular ontology, and building a better NL→FOL translator. The
contribution is the measurement, not the translator.

Each metric's ability to distinguish typed error mutants from meaning-preserving controls of the same base formula.}\n  \\label{fig:perturb}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsection{How Many Peer Families Are Needed?}\n\\label{sec:kcurve}\n\nThe discriminative power of consensus saturates rapidly.\nOn Dataset~E (2,014 items with all seven non-candidate families available), pooled AUROC rises from 0.685 (one family) through 0.757 (three families) to 0.784 (seven families) [ARTIFACT:gen\\_art\\_evaluation\\_2].\nThree families capture 97\\% of the full pool's AUROC.\nThe cross-fitted best three-family pool (DeepSeek, Microsoft, OpenAI) achieves 0.785, matching the full pool.\nNo single family carries the signal: the maximum leave-one-family-out AUROC drop is 0.005.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_kcurve_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Pooled AUROC of consensus as a function of the number of peer families on the development evaluation set (2,014 items, random family subsets). Performance saturates by $k{=}3$, reaching 97\\% of the full seven-family pool.}\n  \\label{fig:kcurve}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsection{Why Consensus Discriminates}\n\\label{sec:mechanism}\n\nThe consensus metric works because correct and erroneous translations exhibit different agreement patterns.\nOn Dataset~E, the mean pairwise agreement rate among translations of the same sentence is 0.760 for correct candidates and 0.159 for erroneous ones (a scatter ratio of 4.8) [ARTIFACT:gen\\_art\\_evaluation\\_2].\nCorrect translations converge on the same logical content despite different surface forms, while errors are structurally diverse: different families produce different wrong formulas for the same sentence.\n\nThe graded consensus score outperforms binary majority voting by $+0.114$ $[0.091, 0.140]$ stratified AUROC.\nBinary voting collapses the continuous agreement fraction into a single bit, losing discriminative information when error endorsement ($e = 0.124$) and correct-candidate divergence ($d = 0.537$) are both far from zero [ARTIFACT:gen\\_art\\_evaluation\\_2].\n\n\\subsection{Negative Results}\n\\label{sec:negative}\n\n\\paragraph{Structural pilot metrics.}\nThe pilot structural metrics (joint conflict, arity inconsistency, shape inconsistency, dangling predicates) achieve AUROC 0.500 to 0.533 on the development screen, indistinguishable from chance [ARTIFACT:gen\\_art\\_experiment\\_4].\nOnly the cross-system predicate-set Jaccard (0.720) carries signal, as a coarser proxy for the consensus approach.\n\n\\paragraph{Formula lint.}\nDeterministic formula-smell detection achieves AUROC 0.508 on LLM outputs: lint rules that fire on human annotation errors (AUROC 0.655) do not transfer to LLM outputs, which produce semantic rather than syntactic errors [ARTIFACT:gen\\_art\\_experiment\\_1].\n\n\\paragraph{Round-trip reformalisation.}\nVerbalising the formula and re-translating to FOL to check Z3 equivalence achieves AUROC 0.513, near chance, because 76\\% of items produce tied scores [ARTIFACT:gen\\_art\\_experiment\\_4].\n\n\\paragraph{Candidate-signature consensus.}\nGiving peers the candidate's own symbol list---intended to reduce correct-candidate divergence---does lower divergence ($d = 0.139$ vs $0.323$ for free peers) but raises error endorsement ($e = 0.459$ vs $0.173$), producing a net AUROC of 0.614 versus 0.770 for free peers [ARTIFACT:gen\\_art\\_experiment\\_9].\nAnchoring the peers to the candidate's vocabulary causes them to reproduce its errors.\n\n%% ============================================================\n\\section{Discussion and Limitations}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n%% ============================================================\n\n\\subsection{Vocabulary Dependence}\n\\label{sec:vocab_dep}\n\nThe principal limitation of consensus is vocabulary dependence.\nTwo formulas with different predicate names are not Z3-equivalent under any identity map, so a candidate using a synonym or a different decomposition than its peers is penalised regardless of correctness.\nOn the perturbation suite, the nonce-rename false-alarm rate is 0.76 [ARTIFACT:gen\\_art\\_experiment\\_8].\nWe tested three approaches to vocabulary-robust equivalence: name-free alignment (exhaustive injective symbol mapping without string similarity), hybrid matching (combining name-based and name-free maps), and gloss-gated checking (verifying renamed pairs with an LLM gloss).\nAll three reduce correct-candidate divergence but proportionally increase error endorsement, producing no net AUROC gain [ARTIFACT:gen\\_art\\_experiment\\_14].\nThe gloss-gated checker failed its development gate (all-stratum AUROC 0.696 vs 0.742 for plain vocabulary alignment).\nThis tradeoff between divergence and endorsement appears structural when the vocabulary is unconstrained.\n\nIn practice, vocabulary dependence is mitigated by standardising the symbol vocabulary in the generation prompt (as in the SIG condition, where consensus reaches AUROC 0.954) or by pairing consensus with a vocabulary-independent text-level check.\n\n\\subsection{Error Endorsement}\n\\label{sec:endorsement}\n\nConsensus cannot detect errors that all peers reproduce.\nOn Dataset~E, 38\\% of errors are endorsed by the majority.\nThe endorsed-error rate is higher for structural errors (57\\%) than for polarity errors (5\\%).\nText-level checks detect some endorsed errors that consensus misses, but the PEER+TEXT fusion does not significantly outperform consensus alone on the development evaluation (stratified delta $+0.011$, not significant) [ARTIFACT:gen\\_art\\_experiment\\_5].\n\n\\subsection{Contamination and Rewrite Invariance}\n\\label{sec:contamination}\n\nThe disguised-judge comparison controls for LLM memorisation of public benchmark data by replacing content words with nonsense tokens.\nThe flash-lite contamination difference-in-differences on Dataset~E is $+0.105$ $[0.006, 0.201]$, suggesting a small memorisation benefit for the judge on some items [ARTIFACT:gen\\_art\\_experiment\\_6].\nConsensus, which uses only Z3 equivalence, is structurally immune to memorisation.\n\nOn the development screen, judges are highly sensitive to meaning-preserving rewrites: the verdict flip rate under contrapositive rewriting is 0.41 to 0.95 for judges versus 0.0 for consensus [ARTIFACT:gen\\_art\\_experiment\\_4].\nConsensus is invariant to any rewrite that preserves Z3 equivalence, but not to vocabulary changes.\n\n\\subsection{Short-Sentence Weakness}\n\\label{sec:short_sentence}\n\nThe consensus advantage over the judge does not hold on short FOLIO-style sentences (CTRL stratum on Dataset~E: $-0.069$ $[-0.23, 0.10]$) [ARTIFACT:gen\\_art\\_experiment\\_6].\nThe method is strongest on long, conditioned sentences where judges struggle with the logical complexity.\n\n\\subsection{Incomplete Confirmations}\n\\label{sec:incomplete}\n\nConfirmation was attempted on three additional fronts: a fresh 550-sentence test set, a second long-sentence sample, and R\\_COMP under free vocabulary.\nAll three were budget-stopped before reaching testability [ARTIFACT:gen\\_art\\_experiment\\_11] [ARTIFACT:gen\\_art\\_experiment\\_12] [ARTIFACT:gen\\_art\\_experiment\\_13].\nThe only confirmed result on an independent test set is the shared-vocabulary long-sentence test (Section~\\ref{sec:main_result}).\nThe Dataset~E result (Section~\\ref{sec:devset}) met its pre-registered criterion but is a development-set estimate.\n\n%% ============================================================\n\\section{Conclusion}\n\\label{sec:conclusion}\n%% ============================================================\n\nCross-family solver consensus is a practical gold-free faithfulness metric for NL-to-FOL translation.\nOn a pre-registered test of templated long sentences with shared symbol vocabulary, consensus outperforms the best cheap LLM judge by $+0.367$ $[0.328, 0.404]$ within-template AUROC, confirmed on a test set independent of all development.\nThe method costs under \\$0.001 per candidate with three peer families, is domain-agnostic, and is structurally immune to memorisation.\nIts vocabulary dependence is the central unsolved problem: when candidate and peers use different predicate names, consensus penalises correct translations and endorses vocabulary-matched errors.\nStandardising the symbol vocabulary in generation prompts removes this limitation, as the confirmed shared-vocabulary result demonstrates.\n\nFuture directions include:\n\\begin{itemize}\n\\item Vocabulary-robust equivalence checks that do not trade divergence for endorsement.\n\\item Extension to richer formal languages (temporal logic, separation logic) where solver-based equivalence remains tractable.\n\\item Scaling the meta-evaluation to domains beyond FOLIO and MALLS.\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\n\\bibliography{references}\n\n\\end{document}\n", "numLines": 417, "startLine": 1, "totalLines": 417}}

for r in sig:

        'lab': r['label'], 'rd': r['matched_reading'], 'k': (int(cls.split(':k')[1]) if cls else -1),
        'p': 1 if r['parse_ok'] else 0,
        'c': r3(r['c_score_sig']), 'np': r['n_peers_sig'], 'ne': r['n_peers_equal_sig'],
        'jd': r3(r['judge_cheap_disg']), 'jo': r3(r['judge_cheap_orig']),
        'ops': '+'.join(r['repair_ops']) if r['repair_ops'] else ''})
cand.sort(key=lambda c: (c['s'], c['g']))

# verify: rebuild c_score from class ids with every slot in the pool
bys = collections.defaultdict(list)
for c in cand:
    bys[c['s']].append(c)
for c in cand:
    if c['c'] is None:
        continue
    fam = slot_list[c['g']]['family']
    peers = [q for q in bys[c['s']] if slot_list[q['g']]['family'] != fam and q['p']]
    eq = sum(1 for q in peers if q['k'] >= 0 and q['k'] == c['k'])
    assert abs((1 - eq / len(peers)) - c['c']) < 1e-5, c

# within-template AUROC on the primary population, must equal SIG.primary
def wt_auroc(rs, key):
    num = den = 0.0
    g = collections.defaultdict(list)
    for r in rs:
        g[sent_list[r['s']]['tpl']].append(r)
    for t, rr in g.items():
        E = [x[key] for x in rr if x['lab'] == 'ERROR']
        C = [x[key] for x in rr if x['lab'] == 'CORRECT']
        for e in E:
            for c in C:
                num += 1 if e > c else 0.5 if e == c else 0
                den += 1
    return num / den

        out.append({'key': k, 'n': v['n'], 'n_error': v['n_error'], 'n_correct': v['n_correct'], 'n_sentences': v['n_sentences'],

    return out

<main id="main" tabindex="-1">
<!-- ================= FINDING ================= -->
<section class="block" id="finding" aria-labelledby="h-finding">
<div class="wrap">
  <div class="grid2">
    <div>
      <p class="q">The question</p>
      <h2 id="h-finding">Can you tell a wrong logic translation from a right one without a gold formula?</h2>
      <p class="lede measure">A sentence can be formalised correctly in many ways, and gold formulas are scarce and often wrong. The paper's answer: ask several independent LLM families to translate the same sentence, and score the candidate by how many of their translations a solver finds <em>not</em> equivalent to it.</p>
      <p class="measure">This is <button class="term" type="button" data-term="consensus">cross-family solver consensus</button>. On the pre-registered test (<span data-bind="sig-n"></span> candidates from <span data-bind="sig-sent"></span> long templated sentences under a <button class="term" type="button" data-term="sig">shared symbol vocabulary</button>) it separates erroneous from correct candidates far better than a cheap LLM judge.</p>
      <div class="bignum" data-bind="sig-delta"></div>
      <div class="bigcap"><button class="term" type="button" data-term="wtauroc">Within-template AUROC</button> advantage over the <button class="term" type="button" data-term="disguised">disguised</button> cheap judge, 95% CI <span data-bind="sig-delta-ci"></span>. Consensus <span data-bind="sig-c"></span> vs judge <span data-bind="sig-j"></span>.</div>
      <p class="measure note">Only this shared-vocabulary test was confirmed on data independent of all development. When generators choose their own predicate names (Dataset E, a development set), the advantage shrinks to +0.099 [0.049, 0.146]. Switch conditions on the right to see both.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="card" aria-labelledby="h-head-view">
      <h3 id="h-head-view" style="margin-top:0">Does the advantage hold under every condition the run measured?</h3>
      <div role="tablist" aria-label="Measurement condition" id="head-tabs"></div>
      <p class="note" id="head-meta" style="margin-bottom:4px"></p>
      <ul class="legend" aria-hidden="true">
        <li><span class="sw" style="background:var(--accent)"></span>Proposed (consensus)</li>
        <li><span class="sw" style="background:var(--base)"></span>Baseline</li>
        <li><span class="sw dash"></span>Chance (0.5)</li>
      </ul>
      <div class="chart" id="head-chart" role="group" aria-label="AUROC with 95% confidence intervals for the selected condition"></div>
      <div class="readout" id="head-readout"></div>
      <p class="note" id="head-note" style="margin-top:8px"></p>
      <p class="takeaway" id="head-take" aria-live="polite"></p>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
</section>

<!-- ================= HOW ================= -->
<section class="block" id="how" aria-labelledby="h-how">
<div class="wrap">
  <p class="q">How it works</p>
  <h2 id="h-how">One real sentence, walked through the metric</h2>
  <p class="measure">The metric needs only the sentence, the candidate formula and peer translations. It never sees a reference formula. Below is a sentence from the long-sentence test set and the ten translations the run's generator slots produced for it. Pick any of them as the candidate and step through what the metric does.</p>
  <div class="card" id="stepper" aria-labelledby="h-step">
    <h3 id="h-step" class="sr">Stepper</h3>
    <div class="ctl">
      <label>Candidate being scored
        <select id="step-cand"></select>
      </label>
    </div>
    <div class="stepper-diagram chart" id="step-diagram" aria-hidden="true"></div>
    <ol class="stage-list" id="step-markers" aria-label="Stages"></ol>
    <p class="sr" aria-live="polite" id="step-live"></p>
    <div id="step-body"></div>
    <div class="navrow">
      <button class="plain" type="button" id="step-prev">&larr; Previous</button>
      <button class="plain" type="button" id="step-next">Next &rarr;</button>
      <span class="note">Left and right arrow keys also move between stages.</span>
    </div>
    <p class="takeaway" id="step-take" aria-live="polite"></p>
  </div>
</div>
</section>

<!-- ================= EVIDENCE ================= -->
<section class="block" id="evidence" aria-labelledby="h-evidence">
<div class="wrap">
  <p class="q">Explore the evidence</p>
  <h2 id="h-evidence">Every candidate from the confirmed test, and where the gap comes from</h2>

  <h3 id="h-browser">What does the metric say about one candidate, and does the judge agree?</h3>
  <p class="measure">All <span data-bind="rc-n"></span> translations of the <span data-bind="rc-sent"></span> R<sub>COMP</sub> sentences in the shared-vocabulary condition. Labels are Z3 equivalence to the sentence's reference readings. The consensus score and the disguised judge's score are both oriented so that higher means "more likely an error"; each flags at 0.5.</p>
  <div class="ctl" role="group" aria-label="Item filters">
    <label>Show
      <select id="ib-filter">
        <option value="all">All candidates</option>
        <option value="ERROR">Errors (label)</option>
        <option value="CORRECT">Correct (label)</option>
        <option value="disagree">Consensus and judge disagree</option>
        <option value="judgemiss">Errors the judge passed</option>
        <option value="fa">Correct but flagged by consensus</option>
        <option value="cmiss">Errors consensus passed</option>
        <option value="other">Reading choice, off-signature, unparseable</option>
      </select>
    </label>
    <label>Template
      <select id="ib-tpl"><option value="all">All templates</option></select>
    </label>
    <label>Sort by
      <select id="ib-sort">
        <option value="c">Consensus score, high first</option>
        <option value="j">Judge score, high first</option>
        <option value="gap">Consensus minus judge</option>
        <option value="sent">Sentence order</option>
      </select>
    </label>
    <label>Search sentence or formula
      <input type="search" id="ib-q" placeholder="e.g. unless, Famous" autocomplete="off">
    </label>
  </div>
  <p id="ib-count" aria-live="polite" class="note"></p>
  <div class="browser">
    <div>
      <ul class="ilist" id="ib-list" aria-label="Matching candidates"></ul>
      <div class="navrow"><button class="plain" type="button" id="ib-more">Show 60 more</button></div>
    </div>
    <div class="detail" id="ib-detail" aria-live="polite"></div>
  </div>
  <p class="takeaway" id="ib-take" aria-live="polite"></p>

  <h3 id="h-break">Does the gap hold in every template and at every length?</h3>
  <p class="measure">Each row is one slice of the primary population, with consensus and the disguised judge scored on the same candidates. Values are the run's recorded AUROCs with 95% sentence-clustered bootstrap CIs.</p>
  <div class="ctl">
    <label>Slice by
      <select id="bk-by">
        <option value="template">Sentence template (T1 to T9)</option>
        <option value="word_tercile">Sentence length tercile</option>
        <option value="nconds_bin">Number of conditions</option>
      </select>
    </label>
  </div>
  <ul class="legend" aria-hidden="true">
    <li><span class="sw" style="background:var(--accent)"></span>Consensus</li>
    <li><span class="sw" style="background:var(--base)"></span>Cheap judge, disguised</li>
    <li><span class="sw dash"></span>Chance (0.5)</li>
  </ul>
  <div class="chart card" id="bk-chart" role="group" aria-label="AUROC by slice"></div>
  <p class="takeaway" id="bk-take" aria-live="polite"></p>

  <h3 id="h-k">How many peer families does the metric need?</h3>
  <p class="measure">On Dataset E, the run drew 50 random subsets of <em>k</em> peer families for each of 2,014 candidates that had all seven other families available, and recomputed the pooled AUROC. Drag <em>k</em> to see what each extra family buys.</p>
  <div class="ctl">
    <div class="lbl"><span id="k-lab">Number of peer families, k</span>
      <div class="rangebox"><input type="range" id="k-range" min="1" max="7" step="1" value="3" aria-labelledby="k-lab" aria-describedby="k-out"><output id="k-out" for="k-range"></output></div>
    </div>
  </div>
  <ul class="legend" aria-hidden="true">
    <li><span class="sw" style="background:var(--accent)"></span>All candidates (band: 2.5th to 97.5th percentile over draws)</li>
    <li><span class="sw sq" style="background:var(--third)"></span>Longest third of sentences (&gt;26 words)</li>
    <li><span class="sw dash"></span>Full 7-family pool</li>
  </ul>
  <div class="chart card" id="k-chart" role="group" aria-label="AUROC against number of peer families"></div>
  <div class="kpis" id="k-kpis"></div>
  <p class="takeaway" id="k-take" aria-live="polite"></p>
</div>
</section>

<!-- ================= TRY ================= -->
<section class="block" id="try" aria-labelledby="h-try">
<div class="wrap">
  <p class="q">Try it</p>
  <h2 id="h-try">Build your own peer pool and pick a threshold</h2>
  <p class="measure">The run kept the Z3 equivalence class of every translation. That is enough to recompute the consensus score exactly in the page: for each candidate, count the peers from other vendors that sit in its class. Untick generator slots to shrink the pool, move the threshold, and the scores, AUROC and error rates are recomputed on the <span data-bind="sig-n"></span> primary candidates. With every slot ticked, the recomputed scores equal the recorded ones.</p>
  <div class="card">
    <fieldset class="checks" id="try-slots"><legend>Peer pool (generator slots)</legend></fieldset>
    <div class="ctl">
      <button class="plain" type="button" data-preset="all">All ten slots</button>
      <button class="plain" type="button" data-preset="three">DeepSeek, Phi-4, GPT-4.1-mini</button>
      <div class="lbl"><span id="thr-lab">Flag a candidate when its consensus score is at least</span>
        <div class="rangebox"><input type="range" id="thr" min="0.05" max="1" step="0.05" value="0.5" aria-labelledby="thr-lab"><output id="thr-out" for="thr"></output></div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="kpis" id="try-kpis" aria-live="polite"></div>
    <ul class="legend" aria-hidden="true">
      <li><span class="sw sq" style="background:var(--err)"></span>Erroneous candidates</li>
      <li><span class="sw sq" style="background:var(--cor)"></span>Correct candidates</li>
      <li><span class="sw line" style="background:var(--ink)"></span>Threshold</li>
    </ul>
    <div class="chart" id="try-chart" role="group" aria-label="Distribution of consensus scores by label"></div>
    <p class="takeaway" id="try-take" aria-live="polite"></p>
  </div>
</div>
</section>

<!-- ================= FAILS ================= -->
<section class="block" id="fails" aria-labelledby="h-fails">
<div class="wrap">
  <p class="q">Where it fails</p>
  <h2 id="h-fails">Three ways consensus goes wrong</h2>
  <div role="tablist" aria-label="Failure mode" id="fail-tabs">
    <button role="tab" type="button" id="ft-0" aria-controls="fp-0" aria-selected="true">Correct but outvoted</button>
    <button role="tab" type="button" id="ft-1" aria-controls="fp-1" aria-selected="false" tabindex="-1">Short sentences</button>
    <button role="tab" type="button" id="ft-2" aria-controls="fp-2" aria-selected="false" tabindex="-1">Vocabulary bridges</button>
  </div>
  <div role="tabpanel" id="fp-0" aria-labelledby="ft-0" class="card">
    <h3 style="margin-top:0">Does consensus punish a correct translation that most peers did not write?</h3>
    <p class="measure">Some templates admit two accepted readings: a weaker one and a stronger one (for example, "unless" read as a one-way or a two-way condition). Both are labelled correct. Most peers write the weak one, so a correct strong-reading translation is outvoted. The bars count correct candidates flagged at score 0.5 or above, computed from the per-candidate records.</p>
    <ul class="legend" aria-hidden="true">
      <li><span class="sw sq" style="background:var(--accent)"></span>Consensus</li>
      <li><span class="sw sq" style="background:var(--base)"></span>Cheap judge, disguised</li>
    </ul>
    <div class="chart" id="fa-chart" role="group" aria-label="False-alarm rate by accepted reading"></div>
    <div class="navrow"><button class="plain" type="button" id="fa-go">Show these false alarms in the item browser</button></div>
    <p class="takeaway" id="fa-take" aria-live="polite"></p>
  </div>
  <div role="tabpanel" id="fp-1" aria-labelledby="ft-1" class="card" hidden>
    <h3 style="margin-top:0">Does the advantage survive on short, simple sentences?</h3>
    <p class="measure">Dataset E strata, consensus against the disguised cheap judge on the same candidates (tiers A+B). L25: at least 25 words and 3 conditions; L20: long MALLS sentences; EXC: exception clauses; CTRL: short FOLIO sentences.</p>
    <ul class="legend" aria-hidden="true">
      <li><span class="sw" style="background:var(--accent)"></span>Consensus</li>
      <li><span class="sw" style="background:var(--base)"></span>Cheap judge, disguised</li>
      <li><span class="sw dash"></span>Chance (0.5)</li>
    </ul>
    <div class="chart" id="es-chart" role="group" aria-label="AUROC by Dataset E stratum"></div>
    <div class="tscroll"><table class="data" id="es-table"><caption class="sr">Consensus minus judge, per stratum</caption></table></div>
    <p class="takeaway" id="es-take" aria-live="polite"></p>
  </div>
  <div role="tabpanel" id="fp-2" aria-labelledby="ft-2" class="card" hidden>
    <h3 style="margin-top:0">Can a smarter equivalence check fix vocabulary mismatch?</h3>
    <p class="measure">Each point is one way of deciding when two translations "agree" on Dataset E. Moving left means fewer errors endorsed by the majority (<button class="term" type="button" data-term="e">error endorsement e</button>); moving down means fewer correct translations outvoted (<button class="term" type="button" data-term="d">correct-candidate divergence d</button>). Lines join each variant to plain alignment, the frozen metric.</p>
    <div class="ctl">
      <label>Stratum
        <select id="tr-st">
          <option value="ALL">All strata</option>
          <option value="LONG">Long pool</option>
          <option value="L25">L25</option>
          <option value="L20">L20</option>
          <option value="EXC">EXC</option>
          <option value="CTRL">CTRL (short)</option>
        </select>
      </label>
    </div>
    <ul class="legend" aria-hidden="true">
      <li><span class="sw" style="background:var(--accent)"></span>Plain alignment (frozen V0)</li>
      <li><span class="sw" style="background:var(--base)"></span>Rescored variants V1 to V5</li>
      <li><span class="sw" style="background:var(--err)"></span>Gloss-gated check</li>
      <li><span class="sw" style="background:var(--ink)"></span>Exact symbol names only</li>
    </ul>
    <div class="chart" id="tr-chart" role="group" aria-label="Error endorsement against correct-candidate divergence"></div>
    <div class="tscroll"><table class="data" id="tr-table"><caption class="sr">Endorsement and divergence per variant</caption></table></div>
    <p class="takeaway" id="tr-take" aria-live="polite"></p>
  </div>

  <h3>What the paper does not show</h3>
  <ul class="limits measure">
    <li><strong>Free vocabulary is not confirmed.</strong> The only result confirmed on an independent test set is the shared-vocabulary long-sentence test. The Dataset E result met its pre-registered criterion but Dataset E was also used for development. A fresh 550-sentence set, a second long-sentence sample and R<sub>COMP</sub> under free vocabulary were all budget-stopped before reaching testability.</li>
    <li><strong>Renames break it.</strong> Two formulas with different predicate names are never Z3-equivalent under an identity map. On the perturbation suite the nonce-rename false-alarm rate is 0.76.</li>
    <li><strong>Shared mistakes are invisible.</strong> On Dataset E, 38% of errors are endorsed by the majority: 57% of structural errors but 5% of polarity errors. Text checks catch some of these, yet PEER+TEXT fusion does not significantly beat consensus alone (stratified +0.011, not significant).</li>
    <li><strong>Every bridge trades one error for another.</strong> Name-free alignment, hybrid matching and gloss-gated checking each lower divergence and raise endorsement. The gloss-gated checker failed its development gate (0.696 vs 0.742). Giving peers the candidate's own symbols lowered d (0.139 vs 0.323) but raised e (0.459 vs 0.173), for AUROC 0.614 against 0.770.</li>
    <li><strong>Templated text.</strong> The confirmed test uses templated sentences with a shared symbol list, which is narrower than real NL-to-FOL, where generators choose their own names.</li>
  </ul>
</div>
</section>
</main>

<script type="application/json" id="data-headline" data-source="experiment_7/results/analysis.json (SIG.primary, SIG.secondary, SIG.frontier); experiment_6/results/analysis_T1.json (metrics_R_AB, a_head_on)">/*DATA:headline*/</script>

<script>
(function(){
'use strict';
var $ = function(s, r){ return (r||document).querySelector(s); };
var $$ = function(s, r){ return Array.prototype.slice.call((r||document).querySelectorAll(s)); };
function data(id){ return JSON.parse(document.getElementById(id).textContent); }
var H = data('data-headline'), RC = data('data-rcomp'), BK = data('data-breakdown'), KC = data('data-kcurve'), ES = data('data-estrata'), TR = data('data-trade');
var NS = 'http://www.w3.org/2000/svg';
var MINUS = '−';
function f3(x){ if (x === null || x === undefined) return 'n/a'; var s = x.toFixed(3); return s.charAt(0) === '-' ? MINUS + s.slice(1) : s; }
function f2(x){ var s = x.toFixed(2); return s.charAt(0) === '-' ? MINUS + s.slice(1) : s; }
function sg3(x){ return (x >= 0 ? '+' : MINUS) + Math.abs(x).toFixed(3); }
function fci(c){ return '[' + f3(c[0]) + ', ' + f3(c[1]) + ']'; }
function pct(x){ return (100 * x).toFixed(0) + '%'; }
function pct1(x){ return (100 * x).toFixed(1) + '%'; }
function nfmt(n){ return n.toLocaleString('en-US'); }
function esc(s){ return String(s).replace(/[&<>"]/g, function(c){ return {'&':'&amp;','<':'&lt;','>':'&gt;','"':'&quot;'}[c]; }); }
function el(tag, attrs, parent){ var e = document.createElementNS(NS, tag); if (attrs) for (var k in attrs) e.setAttribute(k, attrs[k]); if (parent) parent.appendChild(e); return e; }
function txt(parent, x, y, s, attrs){ var a = attrs || {}; a.x = x; a.y = y; var t = el('text', a, parent); t.textContent = s; return t; }
function newSvg(container, w, h){ container.innerHTML = ''; var s = el('svg', {viewBox: '0 0 ' + w + ' ' + h, width: w, height: h, role: 'presentation'}, container); return s; }
function measure(svg, strings, cls){ var g = el('g', {}, svg), m = 0; strings.forEach(function(s){ var t = txt(g, 0, 0, s, {'class': cls}); m = Math.max(m, t.getComputedTextLength()); }); svg.removeChild(g); return m; }
function cw(container){ return Math.max(280, Math.floor(container.clientWidth || container.getBoundingClientRect().width || 600)); }

/* ---------- chart tooltip ---------- */
var ctip = $('#chart-tip');
function showCT(node, html){
  ctip.innerHTML = html; ctip.hidden = false;
  var r = node.getBoundingClientRect();
  var tw = ctip.offsetWidth, th = ctip.offsetHeight;
  var left = r.left + window.scrollX + r.width / 2 - tw / 2;
  left = Math.max(window.scrollX + 8, Math.min(left, window.scrollX + document.documentElement.clientWidth - tw - 8));
  var top = r.top + window.scrollY - th - 10;
  if (top < window.scrollY + 56) top = r.bottom + window.scrollY + 10;
  ctip.style.left = left + 'px'; ctip.style.top = top + 'px';
}
function hideCT(){ ctip.hidden = true; }
function bindMark(node, html, label){
  node.setAttribute('tabindex', '0'); node.setAttribute('role', 'img'); node.setAttribute('aria-label', label);
  node.setAttribute('class', ((node.getAttribute('class') || '') + ' mark').trim());
  var show = function(){ showCT(node, html); };
  node.addEventListener('mouseenter', show); node.addEventListener('focus', show); node.addEventListener('click', show);
  node.addEventListener('mouseleave', hideCT); node.addEventListener('blur', hideCT);
}
document.addEventListener('keydown', function(e){ if (e.key === 'Escape') hideCT(); });
document.addEventListener('click', function(e){ if (!e.target.closest || !e.target.closest('.mark')) hideCT(); });

/* ---------- x axis helper ---------- */
function niceTicks(lo, hi, step){ var t = []; for (var v = Math.ceil(lo / step - 1e-9) * step; v <= hi + 1e-9; v += step) t.push(Math.round(v * 1000) / 1000); return t; }
function xAxis(svg, x0, x1, y, lo, hi, step, title, yTop){
  var sx = function(v){ return x0 + (v - lo) / (hi - lo) * (x1 - x0); };
  niceTicks(lo, hi, step).forEach(function(v){
    el('line', {x1: sx(v), x2: sx(v), y1: yTop, y2: y, 'class': 'gridl'}, svg);
    txt(svg, sx(v), y + 16, v.toFixed(step < 0.1 ? 2 : 1), {'class': 'tick', 'text-anchor': 'middle'});
  });
  el('line', {x1: x0, x2: x1, y1: y, y2: y, 'class': 'axis'}, svg);
  txt(svg, (x0 + x1) / 2, y + 38, title, {'class': 'axt', 'text-anchor': 'middle'});
  return sx;
}
function rangeOf(vals, pad){ var lo = Math.min.apply(null, vals), hi = Math.max.apply(null, vals); lo = Math.floor((lo - (pad || 0)) * 10) / 10; hi = Math.ceil((hi + (pad || 0)) * 10) / 10; return [Math.max(0, lo), Math.min(1, hi)]; }

/* ---------- forest: rows of {label, value, ci, group, tip} ---------- */
function forest(container, rows, o){
  var W = cw(container), narrow = W < 560;
  var svg = newSvg(container, W, 100);
  var vals = rows.map(function(r){ return f3(r.value) + ' ' + fci(r.ci); });
  var lo = o.lo, hi = o.hi, step = (hi - lo) > 0.45 ? 0.1 : 0.05;
  var labW = narrow ? 0 : measure(svg, rows.map(function(r){ return r.label; }), 'lab') + 14;
  var valW = narrow ? 0 : measure(svg, vals, 'val') + 14;
  var rh = narrow ? 50 : 34, top = 8;
  var x0 = narrow ? 14 : labW, x1 = W - (narrow ? 14 : valW);
  var plotH = rows.length * rh, yAx = top + plotH + 6, H = yAx + 48;
  svg.setAttribute('viewBox', '0 0 ' + W + ' ' + H); svg.setAttribute('height', H);
  var sx = xAxis(svg, x0, x1, yAx, lo, hi, step, o.axis, top);
  if (0.5 >= lo && 0.5 <= hi) el('line', {x1: sx(0.5), x2: sx(0.5), y1: top, y2: yAx, stroke: '#9aa0a8', 'stroke-dasharray': '4 4'}, svg);
  rows.forEach(function(r, i){
    var y0 = top + i * rh, yc = narrow ? y0 + 36 : y0 + rh / 2;
    var col = r.group === 'method' ? 'var(--accent)' : 'var(--base)';
    if (narrow){
      txt(svg, x0, y0 + 13, r.label, {'class': 'lab'});
      txt(svg, W - 14, y0 + 13, f3(r.value), {'class': 'val', 'text-anchor': 'end'});
    } else {
      txt(svg, labW - 12, yc + 4.5, r.label, {'class': 'lab', 'text-anchor': 'end'});
      txt(svg, x1 + 12, yc + 4.5, vals[i], {'class': 'val'});
    }
    var g = el('g', {}, svg);
    el('rect', {x: sx(r.ci[0]) - 6, y: yc - 12, width: Math.max(12, sx(r.ci[1]) - sx(r.ci[0]) + 12), height: 24, fill: 'transparent', 'class': 'hit', rx: 4}, g);
    el('line', {x1: sx(r.ci[0]), x2: sx(r.ci[1]), y1: yc, y2: yc, stroke: col, 'stroke-width': 2.5}, g);
    el('line', {x1: sx(r.ci[0]), x2: sx(r.ci[0]), y1: yc - 5, y2: yc + 5, stroke: col, 'stroke-width': 2}, g);
    el('line', {x1: sx(r.ci[1]), x2: sx(r.ci[1]), y1: yc - 5, y2: yc + 5, stroke: col, 'stroke-width': 2}, g);
    el('circle', {cx: sx(r.value), cy: yc, r: r.group === 'method' ? 7 : 6, fill: col, stroke: '#fff', 'stroke-width': 1.5}, g);
    bindMark(g, '<b>' + esc(r.label) + '</b><br>' + esc(o.stat || 'AUROC') + ' ' + f3(r.value) + '<br>95% CI ' + fci(r.ci) + (r.tip ? '<br>' + r.tip : ''), r.label + ': ' + f3(r.value) + ', 95% CI ' + fci(r.ci));
  });
}

/* ---------- paired dots per category ---------- */
function pairs(container, cats, o){
  var W = cw(container), narrow = W < 560;
  var svg = newSvg(container, W, 100);
  var all = []; cats.forEach(function(c){ all.push(c.a.ci[0], c.a.ci[1], c.b.ci[0], c.b.ci[1]); });
  var rg = rangeOf(all, 0.01), lo = Math.min(rg[0], 0.4), hi = rg[1];
  var step = (hi - lo) > 0.45 ? 0.1 : 0.05;
  var vstr = cats.map(function(c){ return f3(c.a.value) + ' vs ' + f3(c.b.value); });
  var labW = narrow ? 0 : measure(svg, cats.map(function(c){ return c.label; }), 'lab') + 14;
  var valW = narrow ? 0 : measure(svg, vstr, 'val') + 14;
  var rh = narrow ? 58 : 42, top = 8;
  var x0 = narrow ? 14 : labW, x1 = W - (narrow ? 14 : valW);
  var yAx = top + cats.length * rh + 4, H = yAx + 48;

  var sx = xAxis(svg, x0, x1, yAx, lo, hi, step, o.axis, top);
  if (0.5 >= lo && 0.5 <= hi) el('line', {x1: sx(0.5), x2: sx(0.5), y1: top, y2: yAx, stroke: '#9aa0a8', 'stroke-dasharray': '4 4'}, svg);
  cats.forEach(function(c, i){

    else { txt(svg, labW - 12, y0 + rh / 2 + 4.5, c.label, {'class': 'lab', 'text-anchor': 'end'}); txt(svg, x1 + 12, y0 + rh / 2 + 4.5, vstr[i], {'class': 'val'}); ya = y0 + rh / 2 - 7; yb = y0 + rh / 2 + 7; }
    [[c.a, ya, 'var(--accent)', o.aName], [c.b, yb, 'var(--base)', o.bName]].forEach(function(s){
      var d = s[0], yc = s[1], col = s[2];
      var g = el('g', {}, svg);
      el('rect', {x: sx(d.ci[0]) - 6, y: yc - 7, width: Math.max(12, sx(d.ci[1]) - sx(d.ci[0]) + 12), height: 14, fill: 'transparent', 'class': 'hit', rx: 3}, g);
      el('line', {x1: sx(d.ci[0]), x2: sx(d.ci[1]), y1: yc, y2: yc, stroke: col, 'stroke-width': 2.2}, g);
      el('circle', {cx: sx(d.value), cy: yc, r: 5.5, fill: col, stroke: '#fff', 'stroke-width': 1.2}, g);
      bindMark(g, '<b>' + esc(c.label) + ', ' + esc(s[3]) + '</b><br>AUROC ' + f3(d.value) + '<br>95% CI ' + fci(d.ci) + (d.tip ? '<br>' + d.tip : ''), c.label + ', ' + s[3] + ': ' + f3(d.value));
    });
  });
}

var setHeadTab = tabKeys(headTabs, function(i){ headSel = i; renderHead(); });

  var all = []; c.rows.forEach(function(r){ all.push(r.ci[0], r.ci[1]); });

  forest($('#head-chart'), c.rows.map(function(r){ return {label: r.label, value: r.value, ci: r.ci, group: r.group}; }), {lo: Math.min(rg[0], 0.4), hi: rg[1], axis: c.stat + ' (0.5 = chance)', stat: c.stat});

  ro += '<span>Status: <b>' + esc(c.status) + '</b></span>';

  else if (c.id === 'devE') t = 'With free vocabulary the gap narrows: consensus (' + f3(m.value) + ') beats the disguised cheap judge by ' + sg3(c.delta.value) + ', yet sits level with the stack of all baselines (' + f3(c.rows[2].value) + ').';
  else t = 'Consensus (' + f3(m.value) + ') is ahead of the ' + best.label.toLowerCase() + ' (' + f3(best.value) + ') by ' + sg3(c.delta.value) + ', and the CI of the difference, ' + fci(c.delta.ci) + ', excludes zero.';

/* ================= R_COMP rows ================= */
var ROWS = RC.rows, SLOTS = RC.slots, SENTS = RC.sentences;
ROWS.forEach(function(r, i){ r.i = i; });
var bySent = {}; ROWS.forEach(function(r){ (bySent[r.s] = bySent[r.s] || []).push(r); });
function fam(r){ return SLOTS[r.g].family; }
function sysName(g){ return SLOTS[g].system.split('/')[1]; }
function isPrimary(r){ return (r.lab === 'ERROR' || r.lab === 'CORRECT') && r.jd !== null; }
var PRIM = ROWS.filter(isPrimary);
bind('rc-n', nfmt(ROWS.length)); bind('rc-sent', nfmt(SENTS.length));
function peersOf(r){ return bySent[r.s].filter(function(q){ return q !== r && fam(q) !== fam(r); }); }
function majorityPeer(r){
  var ps = peersOf(r).filter(function(q){ return q.p && q.k >= 0; }), cnt = {};
  ps.forEach(function(q){ cnt[q.k] = (cnt[q.k] || 0) + 1; });
  var bk = null, bn = 0; for (var k in cnt) if (cnt[k] > bn){ bn = cnt[k]; bk = +k; }
